The consumables in a tool kit are as decisive as the tools, and choosing the wrong chemistry is the commonest reason a repair fails a fortnight later.

Adhesives divide by what they bond and how they cure. Polyvinyl acetate, ordinary white wood glue, bonds timber by penetrating the fibres and, in a well-fitted joint, produces a bond stronger than the wood itself; it needs clamping for around thirty minutes and full strength takes 24 hours, and the exterior grades are labelled D3 or D4. Cyanoacrylate, superglue, cures in seconds by reacting with surface moisture, works best on close-fitting rigid surfaces, and is brittle under impact. Two-part epoxy mixes a resin and a hardener and gives the strongest gap-filling bond across dissimilar materials such as metal to ceramic, with working times from five minutes to an hour. Polyurethane construction adhesive foams slightly as it cures, filling gaps and bonding almost anything, and it is what holds a loose stair tread or a panel to masonry. Contact adhesive is applied to both surfaces, left until touch-dry, and grabs on contact, which means no repositioning is possible.

Sealants are different from adhesives, being designed to stay flexible and exclude water. Silicone is the correct choice around baths, showers and sinks, and the sanitary or mould-resistant grades contain a fungicide; it cannot be painted. Acrylic frame sealant, sometimes called decorator's caulk, fills gaps between skirting, architrave and wall, and can be painted, but it is not waterproof and will fail in a shower. Expanding polyurethane foam fills large voids and must be used sparingly, since it can expand with enough force to bow a door frame.

Tapes are frequently misused. PTFE tape seals plumbing threads. Electrical insulating tape is rated for voltage and temperature and should not be used as a mechanical repair. Duct tape has a fabric scrim and strong adhesive but degrades with heat and time, leaving a residue, and it is genuinely poor at sealing heating ducts. Self-amalgamating tape fuses to itself into a solid rubber sleeve and is excellent for temporary pipe and cable repairs. Masking tape protects surfaces during painting and should be removed while the paint is still slightly soft.

Lubricants deserve one clarification, because the common aerosol penetrating spray is a water-displacing penetrant, not a long-term lubricant, and it washes away existing grease. Use it to free seized parts, then apply the right lubricant afterwards: light machine oil for hinges and mechanisms, white lithium grease for metal-on-metal loads, silicone spray for rubber, plastic and window channels, and dry graphite or PTFE powder for locks, since oil in a lock attracts dust and eventually gums the mechanism solid.

sections.heading: Protective Equipment
sections.body:
Protective equipment is the cheapest insurance in the kit and the item most often skipped, usually on the reasoning that the job is small. The injury statistics point the other way: the majority of domestic tool injuries occur during brief, routine tasks by people who did not consider them hazardous.

Eye protection is the non-negotiable item. The eye has no meaningful defence against a fragment travelling at speed, blinking is far too slow, and the damage is frequently permanent. Impact-rated safety glasses conforming to EN 166 or ANSI Z87.1 cost very little; ordinary spectacles are not eye protection, since their lenses are not impact-rated and their frames offer no lateral coverage. Wear them for all striking, cutting, drilling, grinding and anything overhead, and for handling chemicals, where goggles that seal against the face are better than glasses. Grinding and using an angle grinder demand a full face shield over safety glasses, because grinding discs can burst.

Hearing protection matters because damage is cumulative, painless and irreversible. Sound levels are measured in decibels on the A-weighted scale, and the exposure limit halves for every three-decibel increase. Eighty-five decibels is roughly the threshold for concern over a working day; a circular saw or angle grinder runs around 100 to 110 decibels, at which safe exposure drops to a few minutes. Foam plugs correctly inserted give around 25 to 30 decibels of attenuation and cost almost nothing; earmuffs are easier to put on and take off repeatedly.

Respiratory protection is where household work most often goes wrong, because dust looks harmless. Silica dust from cutting or drilling concrete, brick and tile causes silicosis and lung cancer, and the exposure from a few minutes of dry cutting can be substantial. Wood dust, particularly from hardwoods and manufactured boards containing formaldehyde resins, is a recognised carcinogen. A disposable FFP2 mask, roughly equivalent to the American N95, is the sensible minimum for dusty work, with FFP3 for silica; both require a seal against clean-shaven skin, and a beard defeats them. Better still, control dust at source with on-tool extraction or by wetting the material.

Hands and feet complete the set. Cut-resistant gloves suit handling sheet metal and glass, general-purpose grip gloves suit rough materials, and nitrile gloves suit chemicals; the important exception is that gloves must not be worn near rotating machinery, where they can catch and pull a hand in. Sturdy closed shoes, ideally with a toe cap, prevent the dropped-tool injury that is otherwise a near-certainty over a lifetime of small jobs.

Finally, keep a stocked first aid kit within reach and know where it is before you need it. Blue-coloured plasters are the catering convention because they are visible if they come off in food, and the same logic makes them easy to spot in a work area.

sections.heading: Buying the Kit in Stages
sections.body:
Buying everything at once is expensive and produces a box full of tools you never use. The rational approach is three tiers, purchased as need and budget allow, with each tier fully useful on its own. Large pre-packed sets are generally poor value: they pad the item count with low-quality small pieces and rarely include the two or three tools that actually matter.

Tier one covers the tasks that recur in every household: assembling furniture, hanging pictures, tightening what has worked loose, and dealing with an immediate emergency. Tier two adds the cordless drill and the tools that make larger jobs practical. Tier three covers occasional and specialised work and is often better hired than bought, since tool hire is inexpensive for a one-day job and avoids storing something used twice a decade.

A word on where to buy. Independent trade suppliers and builders' merchants generally sell better tools at lower prices than general retailers, and their staff can tell you which fixing suits your wall. Second-hand hand tools, particularly older hammers, chisels, planes and spanners, are frequently superior to new budget equivalents, since the steel in mid-twentieth-century tools was often excellent and wear is visible. This does not extend to anything with a safety function: never buy second-hand voltage testers, protective equipment, ladders or power tools of unknown history.
ingredients: Tier one, the essential core: a 450 gram claw hammer; a set of quality screwdrivers covering slotted, Phillips and Pozidriv; a magnetic bit driver with a bit set; combination pliers and long-nose pliers; a 250 millimetre adjustable wrench; a 5 metre tape measure; a small combination square; a 600 millimetre spirit level; a retractable utility knife with spare blades; a hex key set in metric and imperial; a torch; and impact-rated safety glasses.

Tier one consumables: an assortment of woodscrews in common sizes; wall plugs matched to your wall type; picture hooks; PTFE tape; insulating tape; white wood glue; superglue; a penetrating and water-displacing spray; and a mixed pack of batteries.

Tier two, the capability step: an 18 volt cordless combi drill with two batteries; a set of twist, masonry and brad-point drill bits; a stud and cable detector; a hardpoint handsaw and a hacksaw; water-pump pliers; locking pliers; a socket set from 8 to 19 millimetres; two G-clamps or quick-release clamps; a small pry bar; a nail punch; a soft-faced mallet; a two-pole voltage indicator; insulated screwdrivers; wire strippers; and a caulking gun.

Tier two consumables: silicone sanitary sealant; acrylic decorator's caulk; two-part epoxy; construction adhesive; sandpaper in coarse, medium and fine grades; filler; and dust masks rated FFP2 or FFP3.

Tier three, occasional and specialised: a multimeter; a basin wrench and a pipe cutter; a plunger and a drain auger; a laser level; a digital caliper; a wood chisel set; a hand plane; a heat gun; a step ladder rated to your weight; and a wet-and-dry vacuum.

Better hired than bought for most households: an SDS rotary hammer drill; an angle grinder; a circular saw; a wallpaper steamer; a floor sander; a carpet stretcher; scaffold towers; and a pipe freezing kit.

sections.heading: Storage, Organisation and Maintenance
sections.body:
A tool you cannot find is a tool you do not own, and the time lost searching is the reason many small repairs never happen. Organisation is therefore part of the kit rather than an afterthought.

The first principle is a defined home for every tool, so that its absence is visible. A shadow board, with outlines drawn around each hanging tool, achieves this instantly and is why professional workshops use them. In a toolbox, the equivalent is foam or moulded trays. The second principle is separation by use, so that the tools for the commonest jobs live together and can be carried in one trip. A cantilever toolbox or a tool bag holding the tier-one set, kept somewhere accessible in the house rather than in a distant shed or garage, means small jobs get done rather than postponed.

Storage conditions determine tool life. The enemy is moisture, because steel corrodes rapidly at relative humidity above about 60 per cent, and unheated garages and sheds swing through the dew point daily, condensing water on cold metal. Keep tools indoors where possible; where that is impossible, a sealed container with silica gel or a low-power dehumidifier makes a substantial difference. A light wipe of oil on bare steel, or a spray of a water-displacing product, prevents surface rust. Lithium-ion batteries should be stored around 40 to 60 per cent charged, away from freezing and away from heat, and never left permanently on a charger that lacks maintenance mode.

Maintenance is mostly a matter of small, regular attention. Wipe tools clean before putting them away, since plaster, adhesive and salt from hands all promote corrosion. Check hammer heads and axe heads for tightness. Replace utility knife blades often. Keep saw teeth from contacting other metal, ideally with a blade guard. Oil pivots on pliers and adjustable wrenches. Sharpen chisels and plane irons on a stone as soon as they stop cutting cleanly rather than persisting with a blunt edge, which is both harder work and more dangerous.

Surface rust that has already formed is usually recoverable. Fine abrasive paper of around 400 grit with a little oil, or a soaked cloth of white vinegar for pitted areas followed by neutralising with bicarbonate of soda solution and thorough drying, restores most tools. Deep pitting on a cutting edge is generally terminal.

Finally, keep the consumables inventoried in a way you will actually maintain. A shallow compartment box of screws, plugs and picture hooks, with the sizes labelled, converts a trip to a shop into a two-minute job, and that difference is what decides whether a repair happens at all. Buying screws and plugs in bulk boxes rather than small packets costs a fraction as much per item and means you are never short by two.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes and Knowing When to Stop
sections.body:
A predictable set of errors accounts for most damaged work, damaged tools and injuries in domestic repair, and nearly all of them are errors of substitution or of pressing on.

Substitution is the first family. Using a screwdriver as a chisel or a pry bar bends the shaft and can snap the tip, sending hardened steel across the room. Using pliers on a nut rounds the corners and makes the fastener far harder to remove afterwards. Using a chrome socket on an impact driver risks fracture. Using a wood bit in masonry, or a masonry bit in tile, destroys both bit and workpiece. The general rule is that a tool used outside its design purpose fails in a way that is sudden rather than gradual, which is why substitution is disproportionately associated with injury.

Force is the second family. When a fastener will not move, the instinct is to apply more torque, which usually rounds the head and converts an inconvenience into an extraction job. The better sequence is to stop, seat the tool fully, apply penetrating oil and wait ten minutes, try shock rather than steady force by tapping the tool, use a longer lever or a breaker bar, and only then consider heat or a screw extractor. Similarly, a screw that suddenly spins freely has stripped its hole or fixing, and driving it harder achieves nothing; the repairs are a larger fixing, a plug of glued dowel or matchsticks in the hole, or moving the position.

Preparation errors are the third family. Measuring once. Failing to check for cables and pipes before drilling, which causes the most dangerous common domestic accident. Not isolating water or power. Not clamping the workpiece. Not reading the fixing packet for the specified drill diameter. Each of these takes under a minute and each prevents a disproportionate amount of damage.

Knowing when to stop is a skill in itself, and there are clear thresholds. Stop and call a professional for anything involving gas, which in most jurisdictions is legally restricted and where an error kills by explosion or carbon monoxide poisoning. Stop for structural work, meaning removing or notching a wall, beam or joist, since the load path may not be what it appears. Stop for consumer units, new circuits and anything electrical beyond your legal scope. Stop for suspected asbestos in any building predating about 1980, which should be tested rather than disturbed. Stop for work at height beyond a short step ladder. Stop when you have taken something apart and no longer understand how it goes back, before removing anything further, and photograph each stage next time.

The final honest test is whether you can explain what will happen if the repair fails. If the answer is a small mess, proceed. If it is a flood, a fire, a shock or a collapse, get help.

guides.safetyNote: Isolate electrical circuits at the consumer unit and prove them dead with a tested voltage indicator before touching any wiring; in many jurisdictions certain electrical and all gas work is legally restricted to registered trades. Buildings from before about 1980 may contain asbestos and those from before about 1978 may contain lead paint, neither of which should be sanded, drilled or broken up without testing and proper controls. Wear eye protection for any cutting, striking, drilling or grinding, and stop and call a professional when structure, gas, water under pressure or mains electricity are involved and you are unsure.
